report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible but overstated. Evidence does **not** establish that simply following a vegetarian diet *causes* longer life expectancy than eating meat. Most evidence measures deaths during follow-up—not life expectancy—and comes from observational cohorts, so differences in smoking, body weight, exercise, alcohol use, income, healthcare, and the quality of both diets can contribute.

One influential U.S. Adventist cohort found vegetarians had 12% lower adjusted all-cause mortality than nonvegetarians (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80–0.97). But Adventists share unusually health-conscious lifestyles and the association was notably clearer in men, limiting generalization. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4191896/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4191896/)

Results are not uniform: a large pooled analysis of British vegetarian cohorts concluded that vegetarians and comparable nonvegetarians had **similar all-cause mortality**. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4691673/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4691673/)

Broader syntheses support benefits for *well-designed plant-rich diets*: a 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis found a potential protective association with chronic-disease mortality, while explicitly noting limitations and need for further research. [https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10408398.2021.1918628](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10408398.2021.1918628) An umbrella review also found evidence of lower ischemic-heart-disease risk/mortality, but this is not equivalent to proven longer overall survival. [https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/15/19/4103](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/15/19/4103)

The strongest takeaway: replacing red/processed meat with nutritious plant foods is likely beneficial; “vegetarian” alone, including diets high in refined foods, is not a demonstrated longevity guarantee.
